kalyan-dighi-baliakandi.desc: Kalyan Dighi is a large excavated pond in Islampur union of Baliakandi upazila and one of the district's local places of interest. Old dighis like this were dug across Bengal by landlords and rulers to store water through the dry season. Today it is simply a quiet spot where villagers bathe, fish and rest in the evening. It makes a gentle detour on a trip to Padamdi.
blocks: From Baliakandi bazar take a local auto; ask for Kalyan Dighi in Islampur union.

glance: 145 km to Rajbari by road, 4–5 hours by bus or car
godar-bazar-padma.desc: Godar Bazar is a stretch of the Padma's bank just outside Rajbari town where locals come to sit by the water. The river here is wide and fast, with chars rising in the dry season. Boatmen offer short rides, and tea stalls line the embankment in the evenings. It is the simplest way to experience the Padma from Rajbari.
blocks: Rickshaw or auto from Rajbari town, about 10–15 minutes.
Riverbank erosion is common; stay back from crumbling edges, especially in monsoon.

goalanda-ghat-curry.desc: In the steamer days, cooks on the boats and at the ghat at Goalanda became famous for a fiery chicken curry, still remembered as 'Goalondo steamer curry' in Bengali kitchens. Today the eateries at Daulatdia serve spicy chicken and fresh Padma fish, especially fried hilsa, to ferry passengers. The food is simple, hot and full of chilli. It is the taste of travelling across the Padma.

glance: 145 km to Rajbari by road, 4–5 hours by bus or car
daulatdia-ghat.desc: Goalanda was once the terminus of the Eastern Bengal Railway, where passengers transferred from train to steamer for Dhaka and Assam. Today nearby Daulatdia is the main ferry ghat linking the south-west to Paturia and Dhaka. The scene is noisy and endlessly busy, with ferries loading buses and trucks and hawkers selling everything from cucumbers to fried fish. Standing on deck mid-river gives a real sense of the Padma's size.
blocks: Any bus between Dhaka (via Paturia) and the south-west stops at Daulatdia; from Rajbari town take a bus or auto.
Keep valuables close in the crowds; take a ferry ride across and back for the river views.

rajbari-bishad-sindhu-heritage.desc: Bishad Sindhu, Mir Mosharraf Hossain's prose retelling of the tragedy of Karbala, is one of the best-known works of Bengali Muslim literature. Rajbari claims the author as its own, since he lived and was buried at Padamdi. Commemorations are held around his birth and death anniversaries. For literature lovers it adds a personal layer to a visit to the district.

glance: 145 km to Rajbari by road, 4–5 hours by bus or car
padamdi-mir-mosharraf.desc: Mir Mosharraf Hossain, one of the pioneers of Bengali prose and author of the much-loved Bishad Sindhu, spent much of his life at the Padamdi estate in Baliakandi upazila. He died here in the early 20th century and was buried in the family graveyard. A memorial complex has been built nearby to honour him. It is a quiet, rural place, best for readers and history lovers.
blocks: Bus or CNG from Rajbari town to Baliakandi, then an auto to Padamdi.

glance: winter (Dec–Jan), spring (Feb–Mar), summer (Apr–May), monsoon (Jun–Jul), autumn (Aug–Sep) and late autumn (Oct–Nov)
rajbari-khir-chomchom.desc: Rajbari's sweet shops make a version of chomchom finished with a coat of khir, milk reduced and crumbled into a sweet, grainy covering. The result is denser and creamier than a plain chomchom. Local shops make many other sweets too, from kalojam to sandesh. Buy them fresh in Rajbari town.

glance: Bazaars in Rajbari town and Pangsha
rajbari-jamun.desc: Rajbari is a major source of jamun (black plum), with large quantities sent to Dhaka every day in season. The ripe fruit is deep purple, sweet and slightly astringent, and stains your tongue. Sellers shake the berries in a pot with salt and chilli before serving. The season lasts only a few weeks in early summer.
